facts.statement: Nedcolbertia was a theropod dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous Valanginian age in the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah.
facts.quote: Nedcolbertia is a genus of theropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (Valanginian-aged) Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah.

facts.statement: Nedcolbertia lived at the beginning of the Cretaceous period, approximately 130 million years ago, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivió a principios del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 130 millones de años, en el Barremiense, en lo que hoy es Norteamérica.

facts.statement: The fossil record for Nedcolbertia spans from 137.05 to 132.6 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Valanginian to Valanginian (137.05 to 132.6 million years ago)

facts.statement: Three theropod skeletons were discovered in 1993 by Christopher Whittle near Cisco in the basal Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah.
facts.quote: Three skeletons of a theropod were discovered in 1993 by Christopher Whittle near Cisco in the basal Yellow Cat Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah

facts.statement: Although announced in 1996 as "Nedcolbertia whittlei", the species was formally described and named Nedcolbertia justinhofmanni in 1998 by Kirkland, Whittle, Britt, Madsen, and Burge.
facts.quote: Though in 1996 it had been announced that the taxon would be named "Nedcolbertia whittlei", in 1998 it was actually described and named by Kirkland, Whittle, Britt, Madsen and Burge as the type species Nedcolbertia justinhofmanni.

facts.statement: The genus name Nedcolbertia honors the American paleontologist Edwin Harris Colbert, who was known as "Ned" to his friends.
facts.quote: The generic name honours the American palaeontologist Edwin Harris Colbert, known as "Ned" to his friends.

facts.statement: The specific name justinhofmanni honors Justin Hofmann, a six-year-old boy from Newton, New Jersey, who won a contest sponsored by Discover Card.
facts.quote: The specific name honoured Justin Hofmann, a six-year-old school boy from Newton, New Jersey, a participant of a contest for children by Discover Card, the winner having a dinosaur named after him.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen CEUM 5071 is a partial skeleton lacking a skull that belonged to a juvenile individual.
facts.quote: The holotype, CEUM 5071, is one of the specimens, a partial skeleton lacking the skull. It belonged to a juvenile individual.

facts.statement: The two paratype specimens, CEUM 5072 and CEUM 5073, are fragmentary skeletons lacking skulls that represent subadult individuals.
facts.quote: The paratypes are the other two specimens: CEUM 5072 and CEUM 5073, both fragmentary skeletons again lacking the skull. They represent subadult individuals.

facts.statement: All three known specimens of Nedcolbertia were disarticulated and heavily eroded because they were exposed at the surface before discovery.
facts.quote: All three specimens were disarticulated and heavily eroded, having been exposed at the surface before discovery.

facts.statement: The paratype specimens, though not yet fully grown, were about 3 meters long.
facts.quote: The paratypes, though not yet full-grown, were about 3 m.

facts.statement: Nedcolbertia possessed a thumb claw that was much larger than its second hand claw.
facts.quote: The thumb claw was much larger than the second claw of the hand.

facts.statement: The femur of Nedcolbertia had a lesser trochanter clearly lower than the greater trochanter and a well-developed fourth trochanter.
facts.quote: The thigh bone had a lesser trochanter that was clearly lower than the greater trochanter; the fourth trochanter was well-developed.

facts.statement: Nedcolbertia lacked an arctometatarsal foot structure and did not have an enlarged second foot claw.
facts.quote: The foot was not arctometatarsal. An enlarged second foot claw was lacking.

facts.statement: The original describers assigned Nedcolbertia with certainty to Tetanurae and provisionally to Coelurosauria.
facts.quote: The describers assigned Nedcolbertia with certainty to the Tetanurae and provisionally to the Coelurosauria.

facts.statement: A 2016 study suggested Nedcolbertia is an ornithomimosaur based on comparisons with remains from the Arundel Formation, Harpymimus, and Nqwebasaurus.
facts.quote: A 2016 overview of ornithomimosaur material from the Arundel Formation of Maryland found Nedcolbertia to be an ornithomimosaur based on comparisons with the Arundel ornithomimosaur remains, Harpymimus, and Nqwebasaurus.

facts.statement: In 2024, Cau suggested Nedcolbertia possibly belongs to Allosauroidea but placed it within Megalosauroidea in his analysis.
facts.quote: In 2024, Cau suggested that Nedcolbertia possibly belongs to Allosauroidea, but included this taxon within Megalosauroidea in his phylogenetic analysis instead.

facts.statement: Nedcolbertia is very similar to its close relatives Ornitholestes and Compsognathus.
facts.quote: Es muy similar a sus parientes cercanos Ornitholestes y Compsognathus.

facts.statement: Kirkland described Nedcolbertia as a "small coelurosaurian related to Ornitholestes" in his report.
facts.quote: Kirkland lo describió como un "pequeño celurosaurio relacionado con Ornitholestes" en su reporte.

facts.statement: The vertebrae of Nedcolbertia were not heavily pneumatized.
facts.quote: The vertebrae were not heavily pneumatised.

facts.statement: Nedcolbertia is classified within the unranked family Coelurosauria.
facts.quote: unranked_familia: Coelurosauria

rejected.quote: The holotype of Nedcolbertia had a length of about 1.5 m.
